title: AP Investigation: ICE Detainee Suicides at Unprecedented Rate — At Least 10 Deaths Since Trump's Return, 7 Since October 2025; Average Age 32; Mental Health Screening Failures Documented at Multiple Facilities
detail: The Associated Press published an investigation on May 27, 2026 finding that detainees in ICE custody are dying by suicide at a pace unprecedented in the agency's two-decade history. At least 10 detainees have died by suicide since President Trump returned to office in January 2025 and ordered ICE to dramatically expand arrests and deportations. Seven of those deaths occurred since October 2025, already the most in any single fiscal year in ICE's history — whereas ICE typically records just one or no suicides per year. Nine of the 10 who died were Hispanic men; one was a Chinese national. Their average age was 32. Most had been in ICE custody for less than a month, and in some cases only days, at the time of their death. The AP investigation documented systemic failures: at least three of the nine facilities where suicides occurred have struggled to meet ICE's own requirement that detainees receive mental health screenings within 12 hours of arrival. Staff at multiple facilities ignored signs of distress, delayed mental health treatment, failed to monitor detainees already flagged as at risk, permitted access to materials that could be used for self-harm, and in some cases placed distressed individuals in isolation — which experts say exacerbates feelings of humiliation and helplessness. The investigation drew on ICE inspection reports, jail records, and expert testimony. A companion investigation by NBC News, published May 21, 2026, had analyzed more than 1,000 emergency 911 calls from six ICE detention centers across the country over the past year, finding 28 involving serious self-harm: one man swallowed a razor blade, another drank cleaning chemicals, and at least three cut their wrists. DHS attributed the rising suicide rate solely to the larger detention population, a claim experts dispute. The AP and NBC investigations come as ICE operates its largest detention system in agency history — 73,000+ individuals — following the October 2025 termination of third-party medical care contracts and the May 5, 2026 closure of the Office of Immigration Detention Ombudsman (OIDO), leaving the system with no independent oversight.

title: Sen. Andy Kim Pepper-Sprayed at Delaney Hall; NJ Gov. Sherrill Delegation Blocked; ICE Agent Caught Pushing Protester Under Tractor-Trailer; Trump Calls Demonstrators 'Paid'
detail: On May 27, 2026, U.S. Senator Andy Kim (D-NJ) and New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill led a congressional delegation to the Delaney Hall ICE detention facility in Newark for a legislative oversight inspection, amid the ongoing hunger and labor strike by more than 300 detainees that had entered its sixth day. ICE and GEO Group refused to grant the delegation entry to the facility. During the attempt to access the premises, Senator Kim reported being pepper-sprayed by federal agents — the most serious incident involving an elected official since demonstrations at the facility began May 22. Governor Sherrill and other members of the delegation were similarly refused entry despite the constitutional prerogatives of Members of Congress to inspect federal detention facilities. ICE and DHS did not respond to media inquiries about the incident. President Trump, appearing at a separate event, publicly characterized the protesters outside Delaney Hall as 'paid' demonstrators, offering no evidence for the claim. Separately, video footage that circulated widely on social media appeared to show an ICE agent shoving a protester into the path of a moving tractor-trailer outside the facility — an incident that NJ officials said they intended to refer to law enforcement. Attorneys for the striking detainees reported that most of the 300+ hunger strikers ended that portion of the protest by the end of May 27, while the labor/work strike continued. The facility's suspension of family visitation, implemented after earlier protests, also remained in effect. Senators Kim and Bob Menendez had requested Senate hearings on detention conditions; the May 27 events drew renewed calls from Democratic members for a Senate investigation.
